text: A turn of the handle looks simple.
Inside Home Soda Machine,
three things make it possible:
pressure, mixing, and cold.
Pull away the enclosure,
and this is the cold core.
At its center is a stainless steel carbonator:
a sealed tank that keeps water
in contact with carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide enters through a port at the bottom.
While gas is entering,
bubbles rise through the water
and collect in the space above it.
As the pressures balance, gas admission stops.
Fresh water comes in from the top.
Look closely at the inlet:
a tiny, one-sixteenth-inch hole
turns the incoming flow into a narrow jet.
The stream crosses the carbon dioxide headspace
and plunges into the water below.
Its impact draws gas into the pool
and drives circulation.
Those moving interfaces give carbon dioxide
more opportunities to dissolve.
The bubbles are the process you can see.
The carbonation you drink
is gas dissolved in the water.
As the level rises, a magnetic float follows it.
At the high-level signal, the refill pump stops.
Now look outside the tank.
This copper coil carries refrigerant.
As it evaporates, it absorbs heat
through the coil and the stainless steel wall.
The refrigeration loop carries that heat away.
Cold water can hold more dissolved carbon dioxide.
Pressure, mixing, and cooling work together,
so the next pour starts with chilled, carbonated water,
ready for a separate stream of flavor at the faucet.
Home Soda Machine.
Cold soda, on tap.
